analysis.problem_summary: Determine whether string t is a permutation (anagram) of string s.
analysis.intuition: Since the inputs consist solely of lowercase English letters, a fixed 26-element array can directly map each character to its offset relative to 'a'. Incrementing counts for s and decrementing for t leaves all elements at 0 if and only if the strings are anagrams.
approach: Initialize a fixed-size integer array of length 26 to store character frequencies.
Traverse string s and increment the array count at index c - 'a' for each character.
Traverse string t and decrement the array count at index c - 'a' for each character.
Check the frequency array; if any entry is non-zero, return false. If all entries are zero, return true.
analysis.why_it_works: An anagram requires identical character frequencies. By incrementing counts for s and decrementing for t, any mismatch results in a non-zero entry in the frequency array.
analysis.key_takeaway: When the alphabet size is small and fixed (such as lowercase English letters), an array-based lookup table avoids hash map overhead and yields O(1) auxiliary space.
analysis.time_explanation: Iterating over both strings of length n takes O(n) time. Inspecting the 26-element array takes constant O(1) time, resulting in overall O(n) time complexity.
analysis.space_explanation: The frequency array size is strictly fixed to 26 elements regardless of input string length, using O(1) auxiliary space.

analysis.problem_summary: Determine whether string t is an anagram of s using dynamic character frequency mapping.
analysis.intuition: Using a Hash Map dynamically links characters to their net frequencies. This approach requires no assumptions about alphabet boundaries and gracefully handles arbitrary character sets like Unicode.
approach: First compare string lengths; if s.length() != t.length(), return false immediately.
Initialize a HashMap<Character, Integer> to record net frequencies.
Iterate through s, incrementing the map entry for each character.
Iterate through t, decrementing the map entry for each character.
Iterate over the map keys; if any frequency is non-zero, return false. Otherwise, return true.
analysis.why_it_works: By tracking net frequency in a map, matching characters cancel out. If any net count remains non-zero, the two strings do not share identical character counts.
analysis.key_takeaway: Using a Hash Map provides flexibility for unbounded character sets (such as Unicode), trading slight memory overhead for generality.
analysis.time_explanation: Iterating through strings of length n takes O(n) time. Each hash map operation runs in average O(1) time. Checking the distinct keys takes O(k) where k <= n, making the total time complexity O(n).
analysis.space_explanation: The map stores up to k unique characters from the input strings, requiring O(k) auxiliary space, where k is bounded by the alphabet size.
